raw_case_text: A 67 years old male, a non-smoker, with history of ischaemic heart disease, status post:coronary artery bypass graft, and bronchiectasis was diagnosed to have angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma (AIBTCL), stage III B at King Faisal Specialist Hospital and Research Centre (KFSH&RC) in Riyadh in late December 2004. He presented with: fever, skin rash, generalized external lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly. The blood counts, blood film and bone marrow biopsy were all normal. The renal and hepatic profiles as well as the immunoglobulin levels were within normal limits. Serological tests for CMV, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), hepatitis C virus and HIV were negative. Computed tomography (CT) scans of chest, abdomen and pelvis showed numerous small lymph nodes in mediastinal, mesenteric and retroperitoneal areas in addition to splenomegaly with focal splenic lesions. Skin biopsy showed atypical lymphohistiocytic changes. A right axillary lymph node biopsy revealed diffuse infiltration with: immunoblasts, lymphocytes, polymorphs, plasma cells, histiocytes and eosinophils with considerable proliferation of small blood vessels. The immunohistochemical stains showed positive: CD1A, CD3, CD4, CD7, CD8, CD15, CD20, CD21, CD30, CD45, CD68 and S100. The gene rearrangement studies revealed a monoclonal T-cell population. The AIBTCL was treated with: prednisone, mycophenolate mofetil and subcutaneous alemtuzumab: 30 mg/month for 4 months. Thereafter the patient developed: CMV infection treated with IV ganciclovir and pulmonary embolism treated with IV heparin then oral warfarin. On 29/10/06, the patient was readmitted with two week history of: fever, cough productive of yellowish sputum and mild dyspnea. He denied any associated chest or abdominal pain, headache or bleeding from any site. Physical examination revealed an unwell elderly male who was in mild respiratory distress. The temperature was 38.7  C, blood pressure (BP): 112/68 mmHg, pulse rate: 92/minute, respiratory rate: 20/minute and oxygen saturation was 93% on room air. There was pallor but no cyanosis, leg oedema, jaundice or external lymphadenopathy. The inspiratory volume was decreased and coarse crackles were heard over mid and lower lung fields bilaterally. There was no abdominal distension, tenderness or palpable organomegaly. Cardiovascular and neurological examinations did not reveal any abnormality. Full blood count (FBC) showed: WBC: 1.83 x 109/L, Hb: 109 g/L and PLT: 315 x 109/L. Differential cell count (DCC) showed neutrophils of 1.1 and lymphocytes of 0.3. Renal and hepatic profiles were all within normal limits. Blood, urine, stool cultures and CMV antigen test were all negative. Chest radiography showed bronchiectatic changes involving both lower lobes and bilateral nodular infiltration consistent with severe pneumonia. The patient was commenced on IV tazobactam-piperacillin: 4.5 grams thrice daily and gentamicin 2 mg/kg IV twice daily in addition to oxygen via mask at 2-4 Liter/minute and IV fluids at rate of 50-80 cc/hour. Initially the patient had partial response then he started to have higher pyrexia and respiratory distress. On 6/11/2006, the patient was experiencing high grade fever and rigors and his BP dropped to 85/45 mmHg. Septic screens were repeated and the IV antibiotics were replaced by IV meropenem 1 gram thrice daily and IV vancomycin 1 gram twice daily. Later on, BP improved and fever started to subside. A repeat CT scan of the chest showed: bronchiectatic cavities involving the lower lobes of both lungs, bilateral nodular infiltration, areas of segmental consolidation and bilateral pleural thickening (Fig. 1). Echocardiogram showed no vegetations, pericardial effusions or valvular defects and brain CT scan showed no evidence of space occupying lesions. Bronchoscopy was performed and BAL fluid showed scattered lipid laden macrophages and gram positive rods identified later on as Nocardia asteroides (N. asteroides). Special stains for fungi were positive and the fungus was identified as Aspergillus niger (A. niger). BAL fluid was negative for acid fast bacilli, pneumocystis carinii, viral cytopathy and malignant cells. Meanwhile, the previously taken sputum cultures grew branching gram positive rods identified as N. asteroides. However, sputum cultures were negative for acid fast bacilli, candida and aspergillus. Aspergillus galactomannan test was positive. Consequently, the following management modifications were made: vancomycin was stopped and meropenem was continued, IV liposomal amphotericin-B (amBisome) 5 mg/kg/day was commenced in addition to oral trimethoprim-sulphamethoxazole (TMP/SMZ) 960 mg thrice daily as well as IV amikacin 15 mg/kg/day. Later on, the patient started to improve clinically and radiologically and oxygen requirements decreased gradually. One week later, the patient sustained his hemodynamic stability and his clinical improvement so IV meropenem was discontinued. On 20/11/2006, IV amikacin was stopped and IV amBisome was replaced by oral voriconazole. Two days later; the patient was totally asymptomatic and his physical examination showed few basal crackles with good air entry bilaterally. FBC showed WBC: 2.25 x 109/L with neutrophils of 1.4, Hb: 94 g/L and PLT: 147 x 109/L. Renal and hepatic profiles were normal. He was discharged on: voriconazole 200 mg orally twice daily and TMP/SMZ 960 mg orally thrice daily for 6 weeks in addition to warfarin, omeprazole, prophylactic valganciclovir as well as ventolin and atrovent inhalers. Thereafter, the patient had regular follow up at the hematology outpatient clinic and he remained clinically stable.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 67-year-old male with stage IIIB angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma and bronchiectasis presented on October 29, 2006, with a 2-week history of fever, cough productive of yellowish sputum, and mild dyspnea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed in late December 2004 with stage IIIB angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma (AIBTCL; monoclonal T-cell population positive for CD3, CD4, CD8, CD21, CD30 on axillary node biopsy) after presenting with fever, rash, generalized lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly, the patient had been treated with prednisone, mycophenolate mofetil, and subcutaneous alemtuzumab (30 mg/month for 4 months), complicated by CMV infection (treated with IV ganciclovir) and pulmonary embolism (treated with IV heparin and oral warfarin). On October 29, 2006, he was readmitted with 2 weeks of fever, cough productive of yellowish sputum, and mild shortness of breath.
subjective.past_medical_history: Stage IIIB angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma (diagnosed December 2004, treated with prednisone, mycophenolate mofetil, and alemtuzumab); prior CMV infection; prior pulmonary embolism on oral warfarin; ischemic heart disease status post coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG); bilateral lower lobe bronchiectasis. Lifetime nonsmoker.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, productive cough with yellowish sputum, and mild dyspnea; negative for chest pain, abdominal pain, headache, or bleeding.

objective.physical_examination: Admission vital signs (October 29, 2006): Temperature 38.7 °C, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg (dropping to 85/45 mmHg with high-grade fever and rigors on November 6, 2006), pulse rate 92/min, respiratory rate 20/min, and SpO2 93% on room air. General and systemic exam: Unwell elderly male in mild respiratory distress with pallor; no cyanosis, leg edema, jaundice, or peripheral lymphadenopathy; decreased inspiratory volume with coarse crackles over the mid and lower lung fields bilaterally; normal abdominal, cardiovascular, and neurological examinations.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission complete blood count and chemistry: Leukopenia and lymphopenia with WBC 1.83 x 10^9/L (neutrophils 1.1 x 10^9/L, lymphocytes 0.3 x 10^9/L), hemoglobin 109 g/L, platelets 315 x 10^9/L (discharge CBC: WBC 2.25 x 10^9/L, neutrophils 1.4 x 10^9/L, Hb 94 g/L, PLT 147 x 10^9/L); normal renal and hepatic profiles. Microbiology: Blood, urine, and stool cultures and CMV antigenemia test negative; sputum cultures grew branching Gram-positive rods identified as Nocardia asteroides (negative for AFB, Candida, and Aspergillus). Imaging: Admission chest radiograph showed bilateral lower lobe bronchiectatic changes and bilateral nodular infiltrates; echocardiogram normal; brain CT negative for space-occupying lesions.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT (November 2006): Bilateral lower lobe bronchiectatic cavities, bilateral nodular infiltrates, segmental consolidations, and bilateral pleural thickening. Fungal biomarker: Serum Aspergillus galactomannan test positive. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): Scattered lipid-laden macrophages; Gram-positive branching rods identified as Nocardia asteroides; fungal stains and culture positive for Aspergillus niger; negative for acid-fast bacilli, Pneumocystis carinii, viral cytopathic effects, and malignant cells.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Severe pulmonary co-infection with Nocardia asteroides and invasive Aspergillus niger (confirmed by BAL fluid stains/cultures, sputum cultures, and positive Aspergillus galactomannan, with Pneumocystis carinii ruled out on BAL) in a profoundly lymphopenic patient with stage IIIB angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma previously treated with alemtuzumab, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisone. Plan and clinical course: Initial empiric IV piperacillin-tazobactam (4.5 g TID) and gentamicin (2 mg/kg BID) failed, and on November 6, 2006, septic shock (BP 85/45 mmHg) prompted escalation to IV meropenem (1 g TID) and vancomycin (1 g BID). Following BAL identification of N. asteroides and A. niger, vancomycin was stopped and targeted therapy was instituted with oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMZ 960 mg TID), IV amikacin (15 mg/kg/day), IV meropenem, and IV liposomal amphotericin B (AmBisome 5 mg/kg/day). He rapidly stabilized, allowing discontinuation of meropenem after 1 week and transition on November 20, 2006, from IV amikacin and AmBisome to oral voriconazole (200 mg BID) plus oral TMP/SMZ (960 mg TID for 6 weeks) alongside warfarin and prophylactic valganciclovir.
